units.title: Form 4 VA Intro: Course and SBA Portfolio
units.intro: This unit introduces Form 4 visual arts. You will meet the two learning strands (appreciation and making), the values and attitudes the course cares about, and the basic SBA portfolio structure (research workbook + artwork / critical studies). Lessons do not use real public exam papers or high-score student exemplars.

lessons.title: Two Strands: Appreciation and Making
cards: Form 4 Visual Arts follows the official curriculum with two main strands: visual arts appreciation and visual arts making.
Appreciation: learn to look at artworks, understand signs and styles, and the historical, social and cultural contexts of art.
Making: learn to use materials and techniques to express ideas, turning experience and feeling into visual form.
Throughout both strands, build an open and respectful attitude toward different cultures and viewpoints.
Write the two strands side by side: on the left, the form and situation you see; on the right, a material and a step you will try. This card explains the method in words.

quiz.question: What are the two main learning strands in the VA curriculum?
quiz.explain: The curriculum emphasises visual arts appreciation and visual arts making.

quiz.question: Appreciation often includes describe, analyse, interpret and ____ artworks.
quiz.explain: A common four steps are describe, analyse, interpret and judge.

quiz.question: What does the making strand emphasise?
options: Using media and skills to express your own ideas
quiz.answer: Using media and skills to express your own ideas
quiz.explain: Making turns ideas and experience into visual form while building skill.

quiz.question: Match each focus
quiz.explain: All three work together in VA learning.

quiz.question: Put the four appreciation steps in order.
quiz.explain: Describe → Analyse → Interpret → Judge

quiz.question: Compare works: left leans “describe what you see”, right leans “making experiment”. One line each.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, say how you practise appreciation and making together. Hint: sentence one is what you notice; sentence two is one making action you will try.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: SBA Portfolio: Research Workbook and Artwork/Critical Studies
cards: School-based Assessment (SBA) usually means one portfolio: a research workbook plus artwork/critical studies.
Artwork/critical studies: about four pieces under one theme; some may be written critical studies (follow school and official guidance).
The research workbook shows theme exploration, study of related artworks, media experiments and reflection on progress.
Assessment focuses on media skills, visual presentation, relationship with context, creativity/imagination, overall theme communication and progression.
This lesson covers structure and learning focus only. It does not provide real public exam papers or high-score student exemplars.

quiz.question: An SBA portfolio usually includes which two parts?
quiz.explain: Official SBA centres on the research workbook plus artwork/critical studies.

quiz.question: The research workbook develops a theme that the student ____.
quiz.explain: The theme is self-selected and developed over time.

quiz.question: Which item should not appear in the lesson demonstration?
quiz.explain: The lesson demonstration does not reproduce real public exam papers or high-score student exemplars.

quiz.question: Match portfolio parts to roles

answer.Artwork/critical studies: Visual works or critical writing under the theme

quiz.explain: The two parts work together to show process and outcomes.

quiz.question: In SBA lab, order the portfolio start steps: seed theme → open research workbook → gather materials → organise artwork／critical pages.
quiz.explain: Pick a theme seed → Open a research workbook → Gather materials → Organise artwork／critical pages

quiz.question: Compare works: left = workbook page, right = artwork photo. One line each on process vs decision.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Use one theme sentence plus two pieces of evidence to show how the workbook serves your artwork or critical study. Hint: the theme says what you are exploring; the evidence can be a draft and one material test.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Art dictionary: keywords and appreciation writing
cards: An art dictionary is a sorting tool. For each keyword write a definition, one example you can see, and how you would use the word in appreciation writing.
Appreciation writing can start from a keyword. Describe the form first, then use the keyword to explain how you understand the work.
One keyword can have two examples. Compare which example makes the meaning clearer, and say why.
This lesson practises structure only. Use a keyword card you write. Do not use a real paper or a high-score exemplar.

quiz.question: What should one dictionary card include at minimum?
options: A definition, one visible example, and how you will use the word
A picture that is not actually there
quiz.answer: A definition, one visible example, and how you will use the word
quiz.explain: A keyword should return to a sentence you can write.

quiz.question: Appreciation writing can describe form first, then explain meaning with a ＿＿.
quiz.explain: The keyword helps you say what you see.

quiz.question: Match the dictionary fields

answer.Example: One place you see it in a work
answer.Use: How you will write it into a critique

quiz.explain: The three fields make a usable card.

quiz.question: Order one keyword card: choose the word → write a definition → find one example → write one critique sentence.
quiz.explain: Choose the word → write a definition → find one example → write one critique sentence

quiz.question: Compare works: keyword and definition on the left, the form you see on the right. One line each — what the word means, and which evidence you see.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Write a mini word card. Hint: the keyword, one definition, and one example you can see.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Art timeline: art movements and ways of presentation
cards: An art timeline puts movements in an order you can compare. For each movement note the period, one formal feature, and one way it is presented.
A way of presentation might be a wall painting, a sculpture, a design drawing, a page, or a projection. The point is how the form meets a viewer.
When you compare two movements, write one similarity and one difference. Do not stop at dates.
A timeline is an intro organiser. Choose the points that matter; you do not need to fill every period. Use your own card, not a real paper.

quiz.question: What belongs in one useful timeline cell?
options: A period, one formal feature, and one way of presentation
quiz.answer: A period, one formal feature, and one way of presentation
quiz.explain: A movement stays tied to form you can see.

quiz.question: When you compare two movements, write at least one similarity and one ＿＿.
quiz.explain: Similarity and difference give the comparison evidence.

quiz.question: Match a way of presentation with what you can note

answer.Wall painting: How the image sits on a building
answer.Page: How image and words are read together
answer.Design drawing: How a plan becomes clear to someone

quiz.explain: Presentation changes how a viewer meets the work.

quiz.question: Order one timeline cell: name the movement → note one formal feature → note the presentation → compare it with the next cell.
options: Compare it with the next cell
quiz.explain: Name the movement → note one formal feature → note the presentation → compare it with the next cell

quiz.question: Compare works: one movement on the left, another on the right. One line each — the formal feature, and how the presentation differs.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Write one timeline cell. Hint: the movement, one formal feature, and one way of presentation.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

units.title: Drawing, Aesthetics and Design Thinking
units.intro: This unit practises observational drawing, composition, aesthetics, design thinking and material exploration, and how you present your ideas. It first builds a foundation in looking and materials, then leads into later theme work.

lessons.title: Observation and Drawing Basics: Line, Shape, Composition
cards: Drawing from observation starts with looking: overall shape and proportion first, details later—not deepest shadows first.
Basic visual elements: line, shape, colour, texture, space. Organising principles: contrast, rhythm, balance, emphasis.
Try compositions such as rule of thirds, diagonal guides and empty space. Different compositions change where viewers look first.
Wucius Wong brought design principles into ink landscape, showing how structure can organise a picture.
Draw your own line-and-shape drill: big shape, proportion, one leading line. Design structure can organise a picture. Use words and your own line study in class.

quiz.question: A better way to start observational drawing is to:
options: Observe overall shape and proportion first
Ignore the subject and invent everything
quiz.answer: Observe overall shape and proportion first
quiz.explain: Stable overall proportions make details easier.

quiz.question: Visual elements include line, shape, colour, texture and ____.
quiz.explain: Space (depth, layers, empty areas) is a key element.

quiz.question: Wucius Wong’s practice reminds us that:
options: Design structure can organise a picture
quiz.answer: Design structure can organise a picture
quiz.explain: He reorganised ink landscapes with geometric/design-based composition.

quiz.question: Match element/principle

answer.Emphasis: Guides viewers to look somewhere first

quiz.explain: Organising principles control how people look.

quiz.question: Order a drawing start: overall proportion → big shapes → main lines → local detail.
quiz.explain: Overall proportion → Big shapes → Main lines → Local detail

quiz.question: Compare works: dense line vs big colour blocks — where is the visual weight, and why?
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Describe your next observational drawing with one sentence on an element and one on a principle. Hint: the element can be line, shape, or composition; the principle can be contrast, focus, or empty space.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Aesthetics, Design Thinking and Material Exploration
cards: Aesthetic/design thinking: define a problem → generate several options → prototype → test/reflect → improve.
Material exploration: try the same theme in pencil, charcoal, ink, collage, etc., and note which medium best serves your intention.
Presentation skills: state your theme, why you chose the medium, and how composition and symbols carry meaning.
Practice: pick one everyday object; make it twice in two media; write three sentences comparing which fits your theme better.
Make your own material chart: name, texture, limit, and the feeling it can carry. Record it with your sample and a short note.

quiz.question: Design thinking is closest to which flow?
options: Submit a final once with no reflection
quiz.explain: Design thinking is iterative and reflective.

quiz.question: In material exploration, record which medium best expresses your ____.
quiz.explain: Medium choices should serve creative intention.

quiz.question: In a presentation you should at least cover:
options: Theme, reasons for medium, and how composition/symbols communicate
quiz.answer: Theme, reasons for medium, and how composition/symbols communicate
quiz.explain: Link ideas to visual decisions.

quiz.question: Match design-thinking steps to class actions (notice／ideate／prototype／reflect).

answer.Notice a problem: Name a situation you want to improve
answer.Ideate: Write a few ways to try
answer.Reflect: Note which try is closer to your intent

quiz.explain: Each step is a class action that serves your design intent.

quiz.question: Order a material explore: touch → quick try → note feel／limits → choose what best carries intent.
options: Choose what best carries your intent
quiz.explain: Touch the material → Quick try → Note the feel and limits → Choose what best carries your intent

quiz.question: Compare works: two material swatches — which texture fits the feeling you mean, and why (one line)?
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Sum up one design cycle in three sentences. Hint: the problem you noticed, what you tried, and which material came closer to your intention.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: November: Design drawing and design thinking
lessons.subtitle: Move from “looks real” to “communicates clearly”—ask who it is for, then draw.

cards.title: Ask the audience first
cards.body: Move from “looks real” to “communicates clearly”—ask who it is for and what you want them to do, then draw.

cards.title: Design thinking in 3 steps
cards.body: Spot the need → sketch several options → deepen one (materials / colour / words).

cards.title: Try two materials
cards.body: Test the same theme in two materials (e.g. pencil + paper collage) and compare which carries the message better.

cards.title: Three design notes
cards.body: In short lines write: who it is for, what you want them to do, and which visual element helps.

cards.title: Classroom practice
cards.body: This lesson practises design drawing and how a theme is expressed. The lesson does not use real exam papers.

quiz.question: A strong start for design thinking is to:
options: Jump straight to a final rendering
Clarify audience and need, then sketch options
quiz.answer: Clarify audience and need, then sketch options
quiz.explain: Clear problem first; then options matter.

quiz.question: Material exploration is for:
options: Comparing which material fits the message
quiz.answer: Comparing which material fits the message
quiz.explain: Two trials show which message lands.

quiz.question: Design notes should name audience, what they should＿＿, and a visual element.
quiz.explain: Audience + action + visual cue.

quiz.question: Match the three things a design drawing should make clear
quiz.explain: Name the audience, the job, and the material before the picture can be clear.

quiz.question: Order one design drawing: ask who it is for → sketch several options → try two materials → write three critique lines.
quiz.explain: Ask who it is for → sketch several options → try two materials → write three critique lines

quiz.question: Compare works: a plan sketch on the left, a material sample on the right. One line each — what should the plan say, and how does the material help?
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Write one design decision in three lines. Hint: who it is for, what it should do, and which visual element helps.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Design drawing, design thinking and materials
cards: This exercise brings design drawing, design thinking and materials into one practice: define the problem, draw options, then test how a material presents them.
A drawing should mark the viewpoint, a sense of size, and which element carries the message. It does not have to be a final piece yet.
When you choose a material, write a limit: it folds, it is clear, it is thick, or it is light. The limit changes the presentation.
Close with three lines: the problem, the option you chose, and how the material helps the message.

quiz.question: A complete round of this exercise includes:
options: A problem, design drawings, a material test, and three lines
quiz.answer: A problem, design drawings, a material test, and three lines
quiz.explain: Drawing, thinking, and materials belong together.

quiz.question: A design drawing should mark viewpoint, a sense of size, and which element carries the ＿＿.
quiz.explain: The element should serve the message.

quiz.question: Match a material limit with a presentation

answer.Thick: It can make near and far
answer.Light: It can hang or fold small

quiz.explain: A limit is a reason for the material.

quiz.question: Order this exercise: define the problem → draw two options → test one material → write three lines.
quiz.explain: Define the problem → draw two options → test one material → write three lines

quiz.question: Compare works: a design drawing with a viewpoint on the left, a material test on the right. One line each — what the drawing makes clear, and what feeling the material changes.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Write the three lines for this exercise. Hint: the problem, the option you chose, and how the material helps the message.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

units.title: Community Looking, Visual Diary and Theme Seeds
units.intro: This unit practises community observation and a weekly visual diary, then draws theme seeds from community-related design or making. You can use photos and objects from everyday surroundings, or materials your teacher provides, and develop a theme in the classroom. It also connects to how Hong Kong artists attend to everyday space. Classroom practice includes photos, interviews, collecting and sketches.

lessons.title: Weekly Visual Diary: How to Observe and Record
cards: A visual diary is a year-long habit: each week record what you see and feel, plus small experiments, in images and short notes.
You can include quick compositions, colour notes, tiny material trials, and one “today I noticed…” line.
The point is not perfect pages but steady observation and reflection—later theme work will use these materials.
Tip: keep one small book or digital folder; date + place + one reflection sentence.
Visual diary — note gently. Four fields: date, place, one observation, a sketch you draw. Lay the page out in your own book. This card names the fields in words.

quiz.question: What matters most in a visual diary?
options: Every page must be a finished masterpiece
quiz.explain: The diary is a process tool for later themes and the portfolio.

quiz.question: Each entry should note date, place and one ____.
quiz.explain: Reflection turns looking into usable ideas.

quiz.question: How can a visual diary be used later?
options: As material for theme development and the research workbook
Only torn up and never reused
As a real public exam paper
quiz.answer: As material for theme development and the research workbook
quiz.explain: Diaries are a store of material for the theme and the research workbook.

quiz.question: Match diary fields to use (date／place／one observation／sketch).

answer.One observation: Keep the point you want to remember
answer.Sketch: Draw the shape and the light

quiz.explain: The four fields together make one visual-diary entry.

quiz.question: Order one visual-diary entry: pause on site → observe briefly → sketch／photo → one key line.
quiz.explain: Pause on site → Observe for a few minutes → Sketch or photo → Write one key line

quiz.question: Compare works: same corner, day vs night — one line each on light／people flow.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Write a mini diary entry as date + place + one observation. Hint: visual diary — note gently, no rush.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Community observation: finding a theme from the environment
cards: Classroom observation: use teacher-provided or already available photos, clips, objects, or sketches in class to record the environment and your learning.
Making can relate to community: public space, neighbourhood routines, local signs—then reconnect to your theme.
Pak Sheung Chuen often uses everyday actions and ready-mades to make housing/space experiences visible.
Lee Kit often uses household cloth and everyday objects to speak about private feeling and space—community and personal life can be compared.

Practice: in class, use teacher-provided or already available photos, objects, or sketches. Note three symbols, objects, or sounds and how each could become a theme question. Describe contemporary works in words and cite a reliable source.

quiz.question: What can classroom observation materials include?
options: Photos, clips, objects, or sketches provided by the teacher or already available
You may only memorise one slogan
Only one sentence copied from the textbook
quiz.answer: Photos, clips, objects, or sketches provided by the teacher or already available
quiz.explain: Use teacher-provided or already available materials in class to record the environment and your learning.

quiz.question: Pak Sheung Chuen’s practice often makes everyday ____ experience visible.
quiz.explain: For example, bagging a flat’s air to respond to cramped housing.

quiz.question: Match artist to focus

answer.Pak Sheung Chuen: Everyday actions / pressure of urban space
answer.Lee Kit: Household objects and private emotional space

quiz.explain: Both start from the everyday, with different focuses.

quiz.question: After gathering community materials, a good next step is to:
options: Ask a theme question you can keep exploring
Demand real exam papers from the platform
quiz.answer: Ask a theme question you can keep exploring
quiz.explain: A theme question drives research and making.

quiz.question: Order community to theme: observe with classroom materials → sort → list possible themes → pick one to deepen.
quiz.explain: Observe with classroom materials → Sort them → List possible themes → Pick one to deepen

quiz.question: Compare works: shop-sign detail vs whole corner — which better seeds a theme, and why (one line)?
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Draft a theme question from classroom community material in two lines: “I notice…” and “I wonder…”. Hint: the first line is only what you see; the second becomes a question you can keep researching.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: November: Getting to know community art — research
lessons.subtitle: In class, learn what community art is, with past cases for reference. You do not need to go out and run a project.

cards.title: Themes in community
cards.body: A community-art theme comes from a real setting — people, places, habits and objects. Start in the classroom, the canteen, the school gate, the way to school, or a memory, and choose one nearby detail to look at.

cards.title: Ask before you shoot
cards.body: Use sketches and notes to look at a nearby detail: a corner of the classroom, a canteen seat, the school gate, the way to school, or a memory. Ask permission before photographing people, and respect privacy.

cards.title: Short interviews
cards.body: A short classroom interview can ask a classmate which thing in the classroom, the canteen, the school gate, or the way to school they usually do not notice. Keep the questions short, leave pauses, and note the key sentences.

cards.title: One insight
cards.body: Take one nearby insight from the classroom, the canteen, the school gate, the way to school, or a memory: a detail you had not noticed before that relates to the community. Write clearly what you see, and why it relates to the place and the people.

cards.title: Classroom practice
cards.body: This lesson is for recognising community art in class. The visual diary continues each week. Practice starts from a nearby detail, for appreciation and insight. The class does not use a real exam paper.

quiz.question: Before photographing people you should:
quiz.explain: Respect and safety come first.

quiz.question: After interviews, use the notes to:
options: Select useful stories for your theme
quiz.answer: Select useful stories for your theme
quiz.explain: Filter what serves the theme.

quiz.question: Visual research often starts with＿＿, sketches and notes.
quiz.explain: Observe first.

quiz.question: Match community-research moves

answer.Looking: Use classroom materials to note people, places, habits, objects
answer.Interview: Short questions, ask first, keep only useful lines
answer.Insight: A community detail you had not noticed

quiz.explain: All three are classroom research for a theme.

quiz.question: Order one classroom study: sort materials you already have → ask before you record a person → hold a short interview → write one insight.
options: Ask before you record a person
quiz.explain: Sort materials you already have → ask before you record a person → hold a short interview → write one insight

quiz.question: Compare works: a sketch on the left, interview notes on the right. One line each — what you see, and one useful sentence you heard.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Write one insight. Hint: first the detail you saw in the classroom materials, then how it connects to a community.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: November: Getting to know community art — develop and make
lessons.subtitle: In class, look at past cases, then use a classroom exercise to turn that recognition into making. You do not need to go out and run a project.

cards.title: Research into making
cards.body: Use a short classroom trial to turn a nearby insight into a making exercise — paper, a pen, clay, or other classroom materials. Write down which materials and skills you use.

cards.title: Leave a trail
cards.body: Leave traces of idea development: word/image sketches, material trials, why you changed course (research workbook).

cards.title: Learn methods, don’t copy
cards.body: When using an artist’s approach: learn the method, don’t copy their images; use legal or self-made references only.

cards.title: Say it in three lines
cards.body: Use three sentences for this short trial: the theme, how you made it, and what you want the audience to feel. Check the short criteria, then self-assess or ask a classmate to write one sentence.

cards.title: Classroom practice
cards.body: This lesson practises ways to develop and make in class, with a short trial and a three-sentence talk. The class does not claim an official public-exam result.

quiz.question: Leaving a process trail helps to:
quiz.explain: SBA research workbooks value process.

quiz.question: Safer use of an artist’s style is to:
options: Learn the method and remake with your subject
quiz.answer: Learn the method and remake with your subject
quiz.explain: Method yes; their image no.

quiz.question: A three-line artist talk should cover:
quiz.explain: Clear intent for the viewer.

quiz.question: A development trace should record the ＿＿ for each change.
quiz.explain: The workbook should show why you changed something.

quiz.question: Match making traces

answer.Three lines: Theme, method, and what you want a viewer to feel

quiz.explain: Traces turn research into visible making.

quiz.question: Order research into a work: choose one idea → try one medium → record why you changed it → say the work in three lines.
options: Say the work in three lines
quiz.explain: Choose one idea → try one medium → record why you changed it → say the work in three lines

quiz.question: Compare works: research notes on the left, one work on the right. One line each — what decision the notes keep, and what the work shows.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Say one classroom work in three lines. Hint: theme, method, and what you want a viewer to feel.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

units.title: Self-Portrait, Artist Research and Theme Development
units.intro: This unit uses self-portrait to explore identity, and practises proper artist research (cite sources, compare views) to start SBA theme development. You can begin from three entry points: self, relationship and story. Lessons do not use high-score student exemplars.

lessons.title: Self-Portrait and Identity: Self, Relationship, Story
cards: A self-portrait is more than likeness: it can speak about identity, bodily experience, roles and social gaze.
A theme can begin from three entry points: self (a curiosity collection), relationship (a family object) and story (conflict or tension).
Frida Kahlo used self-portrait to speak personal experience and cultural identity—the learning goal is how symbols tell a self, not copying a style for marks.
Wilson Shieh paints contemporary figures in gongbi to explore Hong Kong identity; David Hockney often paints family and looking—useful for a “relationship” theme.

Describe contemporary works in words, and note a museum webpage or a reliable encyclopedia as a classroom reference. Add a public-domain historic self-portrait only when the image is rights-cleared. This card does not pretend a missing picture is here.

quiz.question: A self-portrait can explore:
options: Identity, relationships, personal story and social gaze
quiz.answer: Identity, relationships, personal story and social gaze
quiz.explain: Self-portrait is a common entry to theme and identity research.

quiz.question: Theme entry points include self, relationship and ____.
quiz.explain: Story can mean conflict, tension or a narrative line.

quiz.question: Match artist to entry point

answer.Wilson Shieh: Gongbi contemporary figures and HK identity

quiz.explain: All three can inspire self-portrait/relationship themes in different media and contexts.

quiz.question: When referencing artists, the right move is to:
options: Understand how they use symbols, then develop your own view
Copy a work exactly as your own
Only paste images with no thinking
quiz.answer: Understand how they use symbols, then develop your own view
quiz.explain: Research is for dialogue and inspiration, not cloning.

quiz.question: Order a self-portrait start: choose a door → draw a draft → mark one symbol → write one identity line.
quiz.explain: Choose a door → draw a draft → mark one symbol → write one identity line

quiz.question: Compare works: a self-portrait draft on the left, an object tied to identity on the right. One line each — what the pose says, and what relationship the object holds.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Pick Self, Relationship, or Story and write two lines. Hint: the object or experience you chose, then how it speaks about identity.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

WEST-KAHLO-01.credit: Frida Kahlo — Self-Portrait Dedicated to Leon Trotsky (1937)

lessons.title: How to Do Artist Research and a Theme Presentation
cards: Artist-research steps: choose relevant artists → record basics → study form and context → link to your theme → write a personal view with evidence.
Use reliable sources: museums, galleries, textbooks, teacher notes; separate facts from opinions.
A first presentation suggested structure: theme question → self/relationship entry → 1–2 artist comparisons → next media experiments.
The research workbook should show process: drafts, experiments, failures and improvements—not only final pretty photos.
Reminder: no full real exam papers and no “high-score” student exemplars.

quiz.question: Artist research should end with:
options: A personal view with evidence, linked to your theme
quiz.answer: A personal view with evidence, linked to your theme
quiz.explain: Research must serve theme development.

quiz.question: A presentation should include theme question, entry point, artist comparison and next ____ experiments.
quiz.explain: Media experiments turn research into making.

quiz.question: A research workbook should show:
quiz.explain: Progression and reflection matter in SBA.

quiz.question: Match research steps

answer.Link to theme: State what it sparks for your making

quiz.explain: These steps stop research from becoming a dump of facts.

quiz.question: Order one artist study: choose a relevant artist → note a reliable source → describe form and context → link your theme.
quiz.explain: Choose a relevant artist → note a reliable source → describe form and context → link your theme

quiz.question: Compare works: artist notes on the left, your theme question on the right. One line each — their method, and what you will borrow it for.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Write the skeleton of the first presentation. Hint: one theme question, one artist method, and the medium you will try next.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Theme development and a second presentation
cards: The second presentation is about development. Compared with the first presentation, what question changed, what evidence you added, and what you let go.
The research workbook should show the path: an older draft, a newer test, and one sentence on why you changed it.
A usable shape: the question now → new evidence → how you adapted an artist’s method → the next work.
Speak only about your own development. Do not use a real paper or a high-score exemplar.

quiz.question: What is the main difference in the second presentation?

Only reading out a class number

quiz.explain: The second presentation has to show a path.

quiz.question: The workbook should show an older draft, a newer test, and one sentence on why you ＿＿.
quiz.explain: A change needs a reason.

answer.Next step: What the next work will try

options: Look back at the old question

units.title: Art History Intro: Ancient West and Chinese Art
units.intro: This unit uses a compact timeline and keywords to introduce ancient cave art, Egypt, Greece and Rome, plus an introduction to Chinese art. Practise looking at form, function and cultural context, with a brief introduction to calligraphy and painting as visual language (pictographs, oracle-bone script, silk painting). This is an introduction only, not a complete technique course. Lessons do not use real exam papers.

lessons.title: Ancient West: Cave, Egypt, Greek, Roman
cards: Start art history by asking what images solved for people: record, belief, power, beauty or commemoration.
Prehistoric cave images often show animals and handprints; notice space, repetition and ritual feel—not photo-likeness.
Egyptian art often stresses order, proportional rules and afterlife / sacred hierarchy; profile figures and scale hierarchy are common visual codes.
Greek art often seeks balanced, idealised human proportion; Roman art often emphasises realistic portraiture, public architecture and imperial narrative.

Task: for each of the four periods, write one keyword plus one sentence on function. Later you can turn that into a group art dictionary or a personal timeline. Organise form, function, and context in words. A museum webpage is only a classroom reference.

quiz.question: A good starting question for ancient art is?
options: What function and context did the work serve?
Demand a real public exam paper
quiz.answer: What function and context did the work serve?
quiz.explain: Form should connect to function, belief and social context.

quiz.question: Egyptian art often uses proportion and pose to show ____ and sacred order.
quiz.explain: Hierarchical scale and fixed poses are common visual rules.

quiz.question: Match period to a common focus
quiz.explain: Each period has different functions and aesthetic priorities.

quiz.question: An art dictionary / timeline mainly trains you to?
options: Organise keywords, period traits and simple presentation
quiz.answer: Organise keywords, period traits and simple presentation
quiz.explain: Dictionary and timeline are starter organising tools.

quiz.question: Order this intro: cave → Egypt → Greek → Roman.
quiz.explain: Cave → Egypt → Greek → Roman

quiz.question: Compare works: compare two periods in words. One line each — a formal feature, and a possible use.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: For one period, write a keyword plus one function sentence. Hint: the keyword names a form; the sentence says what the work may have been for.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Chinese Art Intro and Calligraphy–Painting Visual Language
cards: A gentle Chinese art entry point: writing and image telling stories together—pictographs, oracle-bone script and bronze motifs are visual communication.
Early images such as Warring States silk paintings often link ritual, afterlife and identity—look at line, symbol and spatial layout.
Calligraphy and painting often share language: brush energy, empty space and rhythm structure a surface, not only ‘correct characters’.
Intro goal: recognise a few visual codes (line, symbol, void) and describe one work’s form plus a possible context in short sentences.
Task: choose one pictograph or vessel motif, draw it once, and write two lines — lines you see, and a possible meaning. Use your own drawing.

quiz.question: In VA class, pictographs / oracle-bone script are best treated as?
quiz.explain: Writing and image form a shared visual-language tradition.

quiz.question: Beyond character shape, calligraphy–painting intro also watches brush energy, rhythm and ____.
quiz.explain: Empty space (void) is part of pictorial structure.

quiz.question: When describing an early Chinese image, include?
options: A real exam stem copied whole
quiz.explain: Criticism needs visible evidence and contextual hypotheses.

quiz.question: Match intro focus

answer.Brush energy: Line and rhythm organise the surface

quiz.explain: Three doors into reading visual language.

quiz.question: Order one visual-language drill: name the sign → trace the line → write the form → write a possible meaning.
quiz.explain: Name the sign → trace the line → write the form → write a possible meaning

quiz.question: Compare works: a pictograph on the left, a vessel motif on the right. One line each — how the line moves, and what it might record.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Write two lines. Hint: first only the line or empty space you see; second a possible meaning.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Chinese calligraphy and painting history intro: Qin–Han to Wei–Jin
cards: This is a compact intro only. For Qin and Han, start with narrative scenes in wall painting, and the visual shift of clerical-script strokes from round to square.
For Wei and Jin, three names are enough to start looking: early Dunhuang story scenes, Gu Kaizhi’s outlined figures, and the rhythm of Wang Xizhi’s writing.
The practice is to describe form: line, density, and how a figure sits in space. This is an introduction only.
Use your own line study or a written description. A museum webpage is only a classroom reference.

quiz.question: What is this lesson trying to do with Qin–Han to Wei–Jin?
options: Work through every technique from the start
Use a few examples to practise describing line, space, and narrative
Copy a full set of stone rubbings as the assignment
quiz.answer: Use a few examples to practise describing line, space, and narrative
quiz.explain: It stays a compact intro.

quiz.question: A clerical-script intro can notice strokes turning from round to ＿＿.
quiz.explain: Round and square are visible form, used as an introductory observation.

answer.Qin–Han wall painting: Narrative scene and where figures sit
answer.Wang Xizhi: Rhythm and density of the stroke

quiz.explain: Three starting points, not a complete history of writing.

quiz.question: Order one intro note: choose one example → describe line or space → write a possible narrative → stop at the compact range.
quiz.explain: Choose one example → describe line or space → write a possible narrative → stop at the compact range

quiz.question: Compare works: a wall-painting scene on the left, the rhythm of a piece of writing on the right. One line each — how the figures or the line are arranged.

quiz.question: Write one compact note. Hint: the example, one formal feature, and one point you see in the form.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Chinese calligraphy and painting history and technique intro: Tang to Five Dynasties
cards: A Tang intro can look at figure, landscape, or writing for openness and order: how the composition leaves near and far.
A Five Dynasties intro can start with texture strokes and ink layers: how foreground, middle, and distance separate.
Keep only a few technique words: line, ink, empty space, near and far. Use them to describe the form you see.
Use words and a small study of your own. Do not copy a famous painting as the assignment.

quiz.question: What does the Tang to Five Dynasties lesson practise?
options: Copy every famous painting, one by one, and hand them in
Describing composition and ink with a few technique words
Handing in a replica that matches a famous painting
quiz.answer: Describing composition and ink with a few technique words
quiz.explain: The words serve an intro description.

quiz.question: A Five Dynasties landscape intro can notice how foreground, middle ground, and ＿＿ separate.
quiz.explain: Near and far are layers you can see in the composition.

quiz.question: Match intro words
quiz.explain: Three words are enough for a compact description.

quiz.question: Order one technique description: Look at the overall near and far → find one main line → note dark and light ink → sum it up in one sentence.
options: Look at the overall near and far
Sum it up in one sentence
quiz.explain: Look at the overall near and far → find one main line → note dark and light ink → sum it up in one sentence

quiz.question: Compare works: a Tang composition feature on the left, a Five Dynasties ink feature on the right. One line each about the form you see.

quiz.question: Describe one work with three words. Hint: choose from line, ink, empty space, and near and far, and give each word one piece of evidence you see.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

units.title: Theme Seeds: Self, Relationship, Story
units.intro: This unit practises drawing a developable theme question from everyday objects and experiences. The three entry points are: self (a curiosity collection), relationship (a family object) and story (conflict or tension). This can sit alongside the visual diary and prepare you for later self-portrait research. Lessons do not use high-score exemplars or real exam papers.

lessons.title: Three Doors: Collection, Family Object, Conflict
cards: Theme seeds work best when they are small and real—start from something you care about, not a vague mega-topic.
Self: gather a small ‘curiosity collection’ (tickets, stones, packaging, old things). Ask: why keep this? which side of me does it show?
Relationship: choose one family object; note who uses it, when, and any rules or memories—objects can narrate relationships.
Story: use a ‘little person’ viewpoint to spot conflict or tension in an environment (crowding, waiting, rules, misunderstanding); sketch scene and feeling.
Draw your own three-door sheet: collection, family object, conflict. Each column gets an object, one question, and a next step. This card lists the columns in words.

quiz.question: Self / Relationship / Story doors mainly help you?
options: Pull theme seeds from lived experience
quiz.answer: Pull theme seeds from lived experience
quiz.explain: The three doors are discovery tools for themes.

quiz.question: The Relationship door often uses a ____ object to tell a story.
quiz.explain: Family objects carry relations and memory.

quiz.question: Match door to practice

answer.Self: Curiosity collection and facets of self
answer.Relationship: Family object and who uses it

quiz.explain: Doors can later merge into one theme.

quiz.question: A better theme seed is usually?
options: As huge and empty as possible
Small, real, and worth sustained exploring
quiz.answer: Small, real, and worth sustained exploring
quiz.explain: Sustainable inquiry fits portfolio development.

quiz.question: Order a seed: choose a door → name the object → write one question → decide a next step.
quiz.explain: Choose a door → name the object → write one question → decide a next step

quiz.question: Compare works: a curiosity collection on the left, a family object on the right. One line each — does it speak about self or about a relationship?

quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: From Seed to Theme Question
cards: Rewrite the seed as a theme question—e.g. ‘How does this family object define care?’ ‘What tension sits in bodies and space while waiting?’
A strong question opens research and making: observe, interview, test media—not a one-word answer.
Next you can keep writing the visual diary, compare artists and try a self-portrait, and test materials.
Mini presentation shape: my seed → theme question → materials already gathered → media I will try next.
Reminder: this lesson teaches structure and method only. It does not provide real public exam papers or high-score student works.

quiz.question: A strong theme question usually?
options: Drives observation, research and media experiments
Must be a copied web headline
Must be a real exam stem
quiz.answer: Drives observation, research and media experiments
quiz.explain: The question is the portfolio engine.

quiz.question: A mini presentation includes seed, question, materials gathered and next ____.
quiz.explain: Media trials turn the question into making.

quiz.question: After finding a seed, the natural next step is?
options: Carry it into the research workbook and develop it
quiz.answer: Carry it into the research workbook and develop it

quiz.explain: Three tracks advance the theme together.

quiz.question: Compare works: the theme question on the left, materials you already have on the right. One line each — what the question chases, and what the materials show.

lessons.title: Extend, wish and assemble
cards: Extend: stretch a seed into a surreal or abstract picture that still answers your theme question.
Wish and imagination: write an “if” sentence, then decide which visual element carries that wish.
Assemble a self-portrait: join found scraps, paper, and an image you made, and note why each material is there.
Choose one of the three paths to go deeper. A high-score exemplar is not the only next step.

options: Still answer the original theme question, with a different presentation
quiz.answer: Still answer the original theme question, with a different presentation

quiz.explain: All three serve the same theme question.

units.title: Exam practice ground: visual presentation of a theme and appreciation writing
units.intro: The exam practice ground teaches structure only: how appreciation writing is organised, how a theme exploration unfolds, and how making chooses a medium and presentation. Use a question framework you write yourself. No real exam papers or high-score exemplars.

lessons.title: Appreciation writing and theme exploration structure
cards: Appreciation writing can use four moves: describe the form you see, analyse how it is organised, interpret a possible meaning, then judge with evidence.
A theme-exploration shape: theme question → materials you already have → one artist method → the visual point you want to present.
Compare the two shapes. The appreciation paragraphs talk about a work. The exploration slots talk about how your own question opens.
Structure only. Do not use a real paper or a high-score exemplar. The practice stays on writing structure.

quiz.question: A steadier order for four appreciation moves is:
options: Judge, copy the prompt, paste a picture, stop
quiz.explain: A judgement rests on evidence you can see.

quiz.question: Theme exploration can start with the question, then list the ＿＿ you already have.
quiz.explain: Materials are evidence you already hold.

quiz.question: Match the structures

answer.Theme question: What you still want to chase

quiz.explain: Appreciation and exploration use different paragraphs, and both need evidence.

quiz.question: Order a short appreciation: describe → analyse → interpret → judge.

quiz.question: Compare works: four appreciation moves on the left, four exploration slots on the right. One line each — which kind of writing that column serves.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

quiz.question: Write four headings on a prompt skeleton you invent. Hint: describe, analyse, interpret, judge. Do not use a real paper or a high-score exemplar.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · not a real paper

lessons.title: Making structure practice and media
cards: A making structure can be four steps: one theme sentence, an audience, a medium, and a way of presentation.
Media practice: try the same theme sentence in two media, then say which one is clearer.
Design appreciation writing can borrow the same four steps: audience, function, form, and material.
Structure only. Do not use a real paper or a high-score exemplar.

quiz.question: The four steps of a making-structure practice are:
quiz.explain: The four steps make the decisions visible.
